sentences.text: Diplodocus is easily recognized by its classic silhouette, featuring a long neck and tail supported by four sturdy legs.
This dinosaur is the most frequently depicted sauropod, appearing in more museum displays than any other species.
It could rear up into a stable three-legged stance using its tail as a prop, potentially reaching feeding heights of about 11 meters.
Despite its massive size, Diplodocus laid surprisingly small eggs and clutches.
Scientists believe these small eggs were an adaptation to reduce risks during the long time required for incubation.
The genus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1878.
The first fossils were discovered in 1877 by S. W. Williston.
Benjamin Mudge and Samuel Wendell Williston collected the initial specimens in 1877 at Garden Park near Cañon City, Colorado.
Skin impressions found in 1990 showed that some species had narrow, pointed keratinous spines similar to those of an iguana.
Diplodocines possessed highly unusual teeth with long, slender crowns that were elliptical in cross-section and ended in a blunt, triangular point.
Up to five replacement teeth were developing within each tooth socket at any given time.
A 1992 study indicated that the longest-necked diplodocids would have required a heart weighing 1.6 tons, which is one-tenth of their body weight.
A 1951 study by Kenneth A. Kermack indicates sauropods likely could not breathe through nostrils while submerged due to water pressure.
A 2011 study refuted the hypothesis that Diplodocus used its neck primarily for sexual display.
Early 2000s bone histology studies suggested Diplodocus grew very fast and reached sexual maturity in just over a decade.
Comparisons between scleral rings of diplodocines and modern birds and reptiles suggest they may have been catemeral, active throughout the day in short intervals.
Researchers speculate that the Diplodocus tail may have served a defensive, noisemaking, or tactile function.
Speculations suggest Diplodocus may have used their tails for defense or to make noise like a whip.
The distribution of gastroliths found with a D. hallorum fossil suggests these animals may have had a digestive system similar to modern birds, with a crop and gizzard.
Diplodocus is the type genus and namesake of the family Diplodocidae.
The type species of Diplodocus is Diplodocus longus, which is considered a nomen dubium.
The Morrison Formation, where Diplodocus fossils are found, dates from 156.3 to 146.8 million years ago.
Diplodocus lived in what is now western North America during the Late Jurassic period.
Since the 1970s, the general consensus considers sauropods as firmly terrestrial animals, browsing among trees, ferns, and shrubs.
Sauropod footprints found in the 1930s disproved the theory that Diplodocus had a sprawling, lizard-like gait.
Matthew Cobley et al. (2013) disputed the idea that Diplodocus could feed from submerged plants, arguing that large muscles and cartilage limited neck movement.
